name: Platform-neutral fallback requirements in AltID procurement
consequences: Shifting procurement toward platform-neutral fallback paths should increase resilience by reducing dependence on a single vendor baseline, while elevating governance requirements and pushing incumbents to demonstrate compliance. Downstream, procurement cycles may lengthen as standards are validated and enforcement processes are established, requiring stronger contract management and risk oversight.
options: Mandate platform-neutral fallback requirements in AltID procurement specs and require formal risk assessments of reliance on Apple and Google platform signals.
Adopt an open, standards-based fallback architecture using FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect that can be verified independently of platform telemetry.
Create an open-source reference implementation and accompanying test plans to demonstrate secure fallback authentication across multiple vendors.
review: Trade-off: procurement cycles may lengthen as standards are validated; gap: enforcement against incumbent resistance and pace of contract updates remain unaddressed.

name: Demonstrator program to prove fallback feasibility
consequences: A credible demonstrator program can de-risk the concept and build stakeholder buy-in, but it consumes limited funding and time that could otherwise support policy work or procurement planning. Downstream, success may raise expectations for rapid deployment that the project cannot meet.
options: Develop a mobile-oriented demonstrator on privacy-respecting Android with FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect to validate a platform-neutral authentication path in isolation.
Create a browser-based fallback demonstrator using hardware tokens and WebAuthn to illustrate independence from mobile OS integrity signals.
Establish a cross-vendor interoperability lab to test end-to-end fallback access within a controlled identity-provider environment.
review: Trade-off: demos stay in lab conditions and may not map to production integration; gap: insufficient demonstration of operator risk, procurement, and deployment pathways.

name: Coalition-building for resilience framing and procurement leverage
consequences: Building a broad coalition increases legitimacy and reduces policy-friction risk, but may slow decision-making if stakeholders disagree on messaging. Downstream, alignment challenges can arise when translating advocacy into binding procurement commitments.
options: Form formal partnerships with civil-society groups, privacy advocates, and researchers to push resilience framing and procurement-neutral language across policy briefs.
Engage Folketinget's digital policy committee early to secure oversight commitments and reduce friction at milestone reviews.
Coordinate with EU partners to align on AltID and wallet standards, creating a joint advocacy position that adds pressure to procurement decisions.
review: Trade-off: coalition-building can slow decision-making and produce competing messaging; gap: lacking commitments from key policymakers to translate advocacy into binding procurement changes.

name: Standards-driven alignment with NSIS/eIDAS and AltID
consequences: Aligning standards strengthens interoperability and reduces platform lock-in, but external validation can slow procurement and create conflicts with domestic timeline needs. Downstream, gaps may appear in how audits are administered and how results influence vendor selection.
options: Push binding NSIS/eIDAS-aligned standards into AltID procurement to require cross-vendor interoperability tests and independent verification.
Sponsor EU-level interoperability studies to craft shared reference architectures for platform-neutral fallback pathways across member states.
Finance independent standards-compliance audits of fallback components and publish results to build credibility with public-sector buyers.
review: Trade-off: external standards validation can slow procurement and reveal gaps; gap: domestic governance and enforcement mechanisms to implement NSIS/eIDAS-aligned tests are not specified.

name: Alternative trust anchors governance for fallback ecosystem
consequences: Establishing governance around a certified fallback path reduces single-point failure and enables multiple providers, but adds administrative complexity and potential fragmentation. Downstream, clear accountability requires funding and formal authorization channels.
options: Propose a governance model for a certified fallback path anchored in public-sector trust with independent oversight and clear accountability.
Define platform-agnostic trust anchors such as national PKI and open-source identity components that multiple vendors can adopt.
Pilot staged deployment with defined service levels and continuity commitments across several identity providers to stress-test resilience.
review: Trade-off: governance complexity increases administration overhead; gap: clear authority, funding, and enforcement mechanisms for a shared fallback ecosystem are not defined.

name: EU procurement harmonization and cross-border adoption dynamics
consequences: Engaging EU-level standards and procurement norms can broaden legitimacy and reduce risk of national lock-in, but may complicate timelines and domestic decision autonomy. Downstream, alignment with EU expectations can demand additional coordination and resources.
options: Engage EU bodies to influence wallet standards and procurement guidelines toward platform neutrality and fallback readiness.
Coordinate with multiple member states to pilot a joint procurement model for fallback authentication solutions and shared evaluation criteria.
Publish position papers that shape European Digital Identity Wallet architecture while preserving national procurement prerogatives.
review: Trade-off: EU alignment may extend timelines; gap: concrete domestic funding commitments and governance rights to act on EU guidance are unclear.

name: Platform-neutral certification pathway for fallback access
consequences: Establishing the platform-neutral certification pathway increases resilience by reducing reliance on a single platform, enabling continuity during platform outages. It also adds integration and regulatory compliance overhead and requires ongoing governance to sustain cross-platform compatibility.
options: Establish a standards-aligned fallback authentication path using FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect across certified devices, documenting interoperability outcomes with AltID.
Embed platform-neutral trust anchors into procurement language and contract clauses, ensuring supplier audits verify independence from Apple/Google signals.
Run a live, non-production pilot across municipal services to test continuity, user experience, and regulatory compliance for platform-neutral fallback access.
review: Adopting a platform-neutral fallback path improves resilience by reducing vendor lock-in, but the complexity and cost of cross-platform integration may erode early benefits unless regulatory support and funding timelines align; the three options leave interoperability milestones under-defined.

name: Procurement reform to reduce supplier-concentration risk in AltID framework
consequences: Shifting procurement to diversify suppliers reduces single-vendor risk and improves continuity. It also extends procurement cycles and increases administrative overhead, and may provoke political resistance from incumbents that slow progress.
options: Propose phased procurement criteria that separate device-entrained trust signals from identity verification, enabling alternative channel validations.
Advocate for procurement blocks that require vendor diversity, including at least two independent platform environments for essential services.
Develop a procurement playbook linking risk appetite to supplier concentration metrics, with transparent escalation paths for fallback-capable designs.
review: Shifting procurement to diversify suppliers reduces single-vendor risk and improves continuity. It also extends procurement cycles and raises administrative overhead, and may provoke political resistance from incumbents that slow progress.

name: EU and NSIS-aligned interoperability advocacy for platform-agnostic identity
consequences: Aligning with EU NSIS and interoperability agendas can unlock broader adoption, but may slow domestic timelines and require concessions on national policy priorities and budget timing.
options: Coordinate with EU working groups to publish Danish positions on platform-neutral wallets, portability, and continuity requirements.
Draft policy notes translating fallback authentication concepts into EU procurement criteria and technical standards for AltID.
Organize a cross-border proof-of-concept with adjacent privacy and security agencies to validate interoperability across ecosystems.
review: Aligning with EU NSIS and interoperability agendas can unlock broader adoption, but may dilute national policy priorities and delay immediate Danish procurement wins; the three options leave domestic sovereignty considerations and budget timing under-addressed.

name: Coalition-building for platform-neutral access acceptance
consequences: Building a broad coalition creates legitimacy and diverse insight, but it can slow decision-making and generate conflicting priorities; the three options fail to specify accountable governance structures and funding commitments within the coalition.
options: Establish a multi-stakeholder coalition with civil society, academia, and regional authorities to co-author resilience and continuity policy proposals.
Launch a formal public consultation and feedback loop to capture user concerns about fallback access and privacy implications.
Securing parliamentary hearings and committee briefings to elevate fallback-platform discussions within procurement reform agendas.
review: Building a broad coalition creates legitimacy and diverse insight, but it can slow decision-making and generate conflicting priorities, risking ambiguous accountability and funding commitments.

name: Standards-driven architectural blueprint for AltID resilience
consequences: Publishing a standards-driven blueprint clarifies components and interfaces, enabling procurement pressure for resilience, yet risks constraining iterative innovation and creating rigid adherence timelines that are hard to adjust as threat models evolve.
options: Publish a standards-compliant blueprint detailing minimal viable components for platform-neutral identity and resilient fallback channels.
Form an open-standards working group to align device trust signals, browser-based access, and wallet interoperability.
Commission independent security reviews of the fallback architecture to identify gaps in chain-of-trust and governance.
review: Publishing a standards-driven blueprint clarifies components and interfaces, enabling procurement pressure for resilience, yet risks constraining iterative innovation and creating rigid adherence timelines that are hard to adjust as threat models evolve.

name: Public-sector continuity simulations and tabletop exercises
consequences: Regular continuity exercises strengthen institutional muscle and reveal gaps early, but they consume budget and staff time that could be diverted to concrete pilots; the three options do not ensure immediate transition paths or formal decision rights from exercises.
options: Conduct regular continuity tabletop exercises across agencies to stress-test fallback authentication under outage scenarios.
Document decision gates and escalation procedures for platform compromise, ensuring clear lines of responsibility and fallback activation triggers.
Simulate supply-chain disruptions and simulate vendor failures to quantify impact on service continuity and regulatory reporting obligations.
review: Regular continuity exercises strengthen institutional muscle and reveal gaps early, but they consume budget and staff time that could be diverted to concrete pilots; the three options do not ensure immediate transition paths or formal decision rights from exercises.

name: Fallback authentication governance for AltID delivery
consequences: Pulling this lever creates a formal requirement for platform-neutral fallback authentication in AltID procurement documents, shaping supplier selection toward resilience. Downstream, governance overhead increases and procurement timelines may lengthen, while clarity on continuity obligations improves risk management.
options: Institute a formal policy mandating platform-neutral fallback authentication pathways in AltID procurement documents and supplier criteria.
Create a cross-ministerial governance board to oversee fallback authentication readiness, with quarterly reviews and decision gates.
Develop a risk-adjusted budget line to fund pilot testing of fallback methods across multiple service domains.
review: Primary trade-off is slower procurement due to governance overhead, and the three options leave unaddressed concrete budgeting and measurable fallback effectiveness.

name: Public-sector interoperability alignment with European Wallet standards
consequences: Pulling this lever aligns Danish requirements with European Wallet interoperability guidelines, reducing cross-border authentication friction and enabling smoother portability for public services. Downstream, governance overhead rises to track EU spec updates, and timelines may be affected if EU roadmaps shift or diverge from national needs.
options: Engage EU-level working groups to map Danish requirements to European Digital Identity Wallet interoperability guidelines and gaps.
Publish a policy brief detailing how Denmark will implement portability and cross-border authentication using European Wallet standards.
Pilot a cross-border test with a trusted Danish identity partner to demonstrate compliance with NSIS and eIDAS2 interoperability rules.
review: Primary trade-off is governance overhead and potential delay to EU-aligned timelines; the options do not specify a concrete plan for budget or regulatory alignment.

name: Diversified procurement pilots with non-Apple/Google partners
consequences: Reducing dependence on Apple/Google by testing multiple platform implementations and a hardware-backed backup path, the lever broadens the solution space. Downstream, integration complexity increases across vendors, contracting risk grows, and initial pilot costs may be higher before standardization.
options: Launch an early-stage pilot contracting with open OS or vendor-agnostic security stack providers to test fallback efficacy.
Solicit a multi-vendor bidding process featuring at least three independent platform implementations and a hardware-token backup path.
Establish a short-cycle procurement sandbox to compare platform-neutral candidates against incumbent MitID dependencies in practice.
review: Primary trade-off is increased coordination burden and higher vendor-management overhead; the options leave unaddressed how to scale beyond pilots within budget.

name: Certified evidence program for platform-neutral access
consequences: Establishing a certified evidence program creates independent validation of fallback approaches and NSIS-aligned pathways, boosting credibility with authorities and partners. Downstream, certification activities require budget and scheduling, potentially delaying milestones and narrowing experimentation tempo.
options: Commission an independent security review of proposed fallback implementations with publicly auditable criteria and transparency.
Create a certification path for fallback access that aligns with NSIS requirements and uses open test vectors.
Publish quarterly demonstration reports detailing security postures, interoperability tests, and remediation plans for fallback pathways.
review: Primary trade-off is certification bottlenecks slowing validation; the options do not specify funding envelopes or performance targets for reviews.

name: Independent hardware-rooted trust anchor exploration
consequences: Pursuing hardware-rooted trust anchors offers a tangible, platform-neutral foundation for identity signaling independent of OS ecosystems. Downstream, hardware supply constraints and user friction risks complicate rollout, with added integration and security-review requirements.
options: Commission a white-paper and small-scale prototype exploring hardware-based attestation as an alternative trust anchor for the fallback path.
Host a standards workshop with hardware-security labs to evaluate practical constraints and interoperability with existing AltID flows.
Prototype a tamper-evident device layer to isolate identity signaling from mobile OS during fallback tests.
review: Primary trade-off is hardware supply risk and user friction; the options leave unaddressed how to achieve scale and ensure standardization across devices.

name: Distributed stakeholder co-design for resilient identity access
consequences: Co-design with civil society and procurement officials builds legitimacy and aligns resilience expectations across stakeholders. Downstream, consensus-building slows decision cycles and can cause scope drift unless clear governance and decision gates are established.
options: Coordinate a structured co-design forum including civil society, privacy advocates, and procurement officials to shape requirements.
Run a scenario-planning exercise focused on outage response, including governance, communications, and service level expectations.
Develop a public-facing road-map detailing milestones, decision gates, and accountability for platform-neutral access work progress.
review: Primary trade-off is time-to-decision and potential scope creep; the options lack explicit decision gates or accountability mechanisms.
